title: Cable assemblies that fail
intro:
Over the past year **8 %** of a supplier's cable assemblies have failed the continuity test (p = 0.08). From each shipment a receiving inspector tests a random sample of **n = 250** assemblies and calculates p̂, the proportion of them that fail.

Check first that np and n(1 − p) are both at least 10. Then find the standard error of p̂, the probability that a shipment's sample proportion is **0.10 or more**, and the range that holds the middle 95 % of sample proportions. Give the standard error to four decimals and the other answers to three decimals or more.

To check your work in the Workbench (Ctrl+B): choose **Sampling distribution**, set **Statistic** to *Sample proportion p̂*, then **Population proportion (p)**, **Sample size (n)** and **Value of interest (x̄ or p̂)**, and **Shade on the figure** to *Above the value (≥)*. Ctrl+L brings you back.

StandardError.says: That is √(p(1 − p)), the spread of a single assembly (1 if it fails, 0 if not). The proportion of 250 varies much less: divide p(1 − p) by n before taking the square root.
You divided √(p(1 − p)) by n. Divide p(1 − p) by n first, then take the square root, which is the same as dividing by √n.

AtLeast.says: That is P(p̂ ≤ 0.10), the area below. "0.10 or more" is the area above: 1 − Φ(z).
You used √(p(1 − p)), the spread of a single assembly, in z. For the proportion of 250 assemblies divide by the standard error, √(p(1 − p)/n).

Lower95.says: That is the middle 90 % (z = 1.645). The middle 95 % is p ± 1.96 standard errors.

Upper95.says: That is the middle 90 % (z = 1.645). The middle 95 % is p ± 1.96 standard errors.

hints: np = 250 × 0.08 and n(1 − p) = 250 × 0.92: if both are at least 10, p̂ is close to normal with mean p.
The standard error of p̂ is √(p(1 − p)/n) with p = 0.08 and n = 250. Then z = (0.10 − 0.08) / (standard error), and P(p̂ ≥ 0.10) = 1 − Φ(z): stats.norm.sf(z) or pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE).
The middle 95 % of a normal distribution is its mean ± 1.96 standard deviations. Here the mean is p and the standard deviation of p̂ is the standard error.
